operations.evidence: Quarterly fire and rescue incident statistics cover incidents attended by fire and rescue services in England for the year ending March 2026.
Attendance statistics do not measure all fires or emergencies that were not attended or recorded.
Fire data were collected through the Incident Recording System until November 2025 and through the Fire and Rescue Data Platform from November 2025.
A source-system transition can affect comparability and requires explicit period handling.
Attended incidents are categorised as fires, non-fire incidents and fire false alarms.
The three headline categories do not provide an exact parcel-level hazard classification.
A primary fire meets at least one criterion involving a non-derelict building, vehicle or structure, a fatality, casualty or rescue, or attendance by at least five pumping appliances.
The definition does not establish the severity of a specific property without incident-level evidence.
Secondary fires are generally small outdoor fires not involving people or property.
A secondary-fire label must not be assigned to an unobserved local event.
Chimney fires are fires in non-industrial buildings where flame is contained within the chimney structure.
A chimney-fire category does not prove building condition or future risk.
Hot and dry weather can cause higher outdoor primary and secondary fire totals.
Weather-linked annual variation must not be interpreted as a permanent local risk change.
The release defines purpose-built high-rise flats or maisonettes as buildings of 10 or more storeys.
This statistical threshold is not interchangeable with every legal higher-risk-building definition.
A fire false alarm is an attendance where the service believes there is a fire but finds that no such fire exists or existed.
A false-alarm record does not prove malicious behaviour or equipment failure without its subtype.
Fire false alarms are grouped as due to apparatus, good intent or malicious.
The subtype classification must not be inferred from an aggregate total.
Non-fire incidents include activities such as flooding, road traffic collisions, animal assistance and assistance to other agencies.
A non-fire attendance is not itself evidence of fire risk at a parcel.
Recent releases group non-fire incident types into fewer categories based on existing FaRDaP categories without changing underlying definitions or coverage.
Presentation changes must not be mistaken for real incident growth or decline.
Collaboration incidents include assisting other agencies, effecting entry or exit, and suicide or suicide attempts.
Grouped collaboration counts should not be attributed to one component without detailed data.
Medical incidents include first-responder and co-responder categories.
Medical attendance totals do not measure the full demand on ambulance or health services.
Road traffic collisions attended by fire and rescue services are counted within non-fire incidents.
FRS road-traffic-collision counts are not the same population as all police-reported road casualties.
A fire-related fatality is one that would not otherwise have occurred without the fire, and statistical releases include records where the role of fire is recorded as not known.
The inclusion rule requires caution when comparing with other mortality definitions.
A non-fatal casualty is a casualty resulting from a fire whether or not the injury itself was caused by the fire.
The definition is broader than injuries directly caused by flames or smoke.
FaRDaP is continually updated, so published figures may differ from local fire and rescue service records and may be revised.
A published figure must be versioned and must not be treated as immutable.
Fire-related fatality counts are prone to year-on-year fluctuations because the numbers are relatively small.
Small-number changes should not be converted into precise local trend scores.
Suffolk fire and rescue service could not submit all incidents between September 2024 and June 2025 for technical reasons, so figures for that period are an underestimate.
Incomplete regional submission prevents exact local comparison for the affected period.
